narrative:
The model predicted a 62.9% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The three factors that mattered most in this decision were your undergraduate grades in the first and third years of law school, followed by your undergraduate GPA. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest drivers pushing the prediction toward failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average of roughly sixth and fifth decile among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings strongly signaled future difficulty passing the bar.

Surprisingly, your undergraduate GPA of 3.70 actually worked in your favor. It is well above the 3.23 average of accepted students and pulled the prediction toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the negative impact of your law-school class standings.

Your low family income, 22 on the LSAT, and full-time work plans also contributed to the risk profile, but they carried less weight than the three factors above.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your class rank in the remaining years of law school. Stronger performance there would directly address the biggest reasons for the current rejection. Consider seeking academic support or study strategies that have helped other students move out of the bottom decile.
